A sahib is a person of authority, rank, or high social standing who is treated with great respect and deference — specifically, in the South Asian context, it most strongly refers to a European (and especially British) man during the colonial era in India.

"Sahib" is a respectful title meaning master, lord, or sir. When you called someone a sahib, you were placing them above you in social rank. It was not merely polite — it carried the weight of real power. The person being addressed was someone you served, obeyed, or answered to.

Think of it this way: if "sir" is a polite nod, "sahib" was a full bow.
How it was used in colonial India — the most important context

The word became deeply associated with British colonial rule in India. When India was under British rule, Indian people used "sahib" when addressing European men — their bosses, officers, landlords, and rulers. It was the word a servant used to address his employer. It was the word a soldier used to address a British officer. It was the word a villager used when speaking to any white man who walked into the room.

The word wasn't just respectful — it carried an entire system of power within it. The sahib was the one who gave orders; everyone else followed them. So "sahib" didn't just mean "respected man" — it meant the kind of man whose authority you don't question.

The classic image: an Indian servant approaching a British officer and saying, "Yes, sahib" or "As you wish, sahib." That usage captures the word perfectly.

Importantly, it was used both directly (talking to the person: "Yes, sahib") and as a reference (talking about the person: "The sahib wants his dinner" or "The sahib is not to be disturbed"). This shows it functioned as both a form of address and a title.

Sahib was often attached after a person's name as an honorific, the way we might say "Mr." before a name in English. So instead of saying "Mr. Wilson," an Indian speaker might say "Wilson sahib." This construction — name + sahib — was extremely common and is still heard today in parts of South Asia when addressing someone of higher standing.

Since sahib signaled rank, it could be modified to indicate how big that rank was:

  • Burra sahib ("burra" meaning big or great) — the top man, the chief, the most important authority figure. If a company had a manager, the owner above him was the burra sahib.
  • Chota sahib ("chota" meaning small or junior) — a lower-ranking officer or a younger person in authority. Still a sahib, but not the top one.

This shows that "sahib" wasn't a flat label — it existed on a scale of power, and people knew exactly where someone stood based on how they referred to them.

European women in colonial India were addressed as memsahib — a combination of "mem" (from "ma'am" or "madam") and "sahib." A memsahib was the European mistress of a household, with the same air of authority over Indian servants that a sahib had. This word confirms that "sahib" wasn't strictly about gender — it was about race, class, and colonial power — and once adapted, it applied to women too.

Here is something important: "sahib" is not a neutral word. It is charged with the assumption that some people are naturally superior to others. When an Indian person in colonial times said "sahib," they were acknowledging — willingly or by social pressure — that the other person belonged to a ruling class. The word quietly enforced a hierarchy. This is why the word carries a complicated feeling even today. It was respectful on the surface, but underneath, it was a marker of colonial inequality.

Over time, it became possible to use "sahib" in a slightly sarcastic or mocking tone — to describe someone who acts like they're above others, who demands deference they don't deserve. If you said, "Oh, here comes the sahib," with the right tone of voice, you weren't paying a compliment — you were rolling your eyes at someone's arrogance.

Because the word belongs so naturally to the world of colonial India, it appears constantly in books set in that time and place. Rudyard Kipling's stories are full of sahibs. E.M. Forster's A Passage to India uses it throughout. It became, in the Western literary imagination, almost a symbol of the British Empire itself — a single word that conjured the whole relationship between ruler and ruled.

The word is still alive, especially in Pakistan, parts of North India, and Bangladesh. In these contexts, it functions as a formal and respectful term of address — something like "sir" in English. Politicians, senior officials, and respected elders are sometimes called sahib. It has lost much of its racial colonial meaning in everyday use, but its flavor of authority and deference has never fully gone away.

In casual modern usage among South Asians, "sahib" can also be used humorously or ironically to describe someone who acts high and mighty or expects to be waited on — much like calling someone "your highness" sarcastically in English.

A sahib is a person of authority and high social standing addressed with deep respect — historically, the word referred specifically to European (especially British) men in colonial India who held power over Indian people. It sat at the center of a whole system of colonial hierarchy. Today, it survives as a formal respectful address in parts of South Asia and occasionally as ironic commentary on someone who thinks too highly of themselves.
